what_it_does: This paper addresses a critical memory security vulnerability called Rowhammer, where repeatedly accessing the same row in DRAM causes bit flips in adjacent rows, potentially allowing attackers to corrupt data or escape security sandboxes. Modern DRAM implements directed refresh management (DRFM), a standard defense that requires pausing multiple memory banks simultaneously during refresh operations. These pauses occur frequently and cause severe performance slowdowns (up to 49 percent) in real systems. The paper proposes two optimizations: delaying some refreshes so pauses can be batched together, and using a clever counter scheme that tracks aggressor rows with 8 times less storage than prior approaches while remaining compatible with DRFM.
